profile.title: Nutrition Assessment and Counseling in Precontemplation: A 52-Year-Old Woman with Prediabetes, Obesity, Fibromyalgia, and Hidden Nighttime Binge Eating After Pregnancy Loss
profile.summary: This case portrays Lilia Galindo, a 52-year-old woman with prediabetes, obesity, fibromyalgia, and chronic low back pain, referred (not self-requested) for nutrition counseling. She presents in precontemplation, dismissing any link between her diet and her health, and the case trains students in motivational interviewing with a resistant patient, adaptation of nutrition education for low health literacy, and gentle exploration of a hidden nighttime binge-eating pattern rooted in unresolved grief after a 2023 miscarriage. A built-in mismatch between her stated breakfast-skipping today and a prior chart note documenting 'three meals a day' (alongside near-daily acetaminophen refills) teaches learners to notice and reconcile patient-versus-chart discrepancies without confrontation.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in East Rutherford, New Jersey, in her bedroom with the TV visible in the background

patient.name: Lilia Galindo
patient.occupation: Not in the labor force; disabled from working due to chronic pain and fibromyalgia; previously a laundromat attendant
patient.language: Spanish-dominant; speaks limited English, prefers simple spoken explanations over numbers or charts
patient.appearance: Obese body habitus with weight centered around the abdomen; sits stiffly on a couch in a cluttered bedroom with a small TV on in the background; pale conjunctiva and slightly pale nail beds; moves slowly and winces when shifting position, periodically rubbing her lower back; arms crossed, flat affect, checking the clock

persona.personality: Blunt, impatient, no-nonsense; wants answers fast and gets irritated by anything that sounds like a lecture. Underneath the flat affect is some guardedness about things she doesn't want to talk about.
persona.communicationStyle: Short, clipped answers at first. Mixes English with Spanish-inflected phrasing. Dislikes being lectured or shown numbers/charts. Warms up only slightly if a question is rephrased and asked again later with warmth instead of pressure. Crosses her arms, checks the clock, flat tone.
persona.emotionalState: Irritated and resigned about being sent to this visit; guarded; underneath, carrying some unspoken grief and shame she keeps tightly contained.
persona.background: Lilia grew up in a working-class Hispanic family where big family meals were a given, but these days she lives in a crowded house of six where everyone eats on their own schedule, so cooking for just herself never felt worth the effort. She used to work as a laundromat attendant until chronic pain and fibromyalgia forced her to stop. She has a partner who checks on her often, which she finds both touching and exhausting, affectionately grumbling that he's her 'gallina clueca' (mother hen). She keeps a small TV on in her room at night, mostly for company during the hours she can't sleep.
speechExamples: I don't see why this matters, my numbers aren't even that bad.
Everybody's gotta eat something, I don't know what you want me to say.
Can you just say it simple? I don't do good with all that number stuff.
My back is the problem, not what's on my plate.
He's always asking if I ate, if I took my pills — mi gallina clueca, I tell him, I'm fine.
concerns: Being told she has to change everything about how she eats
Being judged for eating convenience food
Having to come back for more visits like this one

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition assessment with Lilia Galindo, a 52-year-old woman referred by her physician for a visit related to prediabetes and weight. She did not request this visit herself. This is an initial nutrition assessment: gather a diet history, screen for barriers to eating well, review relevant anthropometrics and labs, and begin patient-centered counseling. She may be short with you at first.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referred for nutrition counseling related to prediabetes and weight; patient reports her main problem is chronic back pain, not her diet
scenario.openingLine: The doctor sent me. I don't really know why I'm here, I eat fine.
tasks: Take a focused diet history (meal pattern, typical foods, beverages, portions) and identify barriers to healthy eating
Review relevant anthropometrics and labs with the patient in plain, non-numeric language appropriate to her health literacy
Reconcile any inconsistencies you notice between what the patient reports today and what is documented in her chart
Formulate a nutrition diagnosis based on your assessment findings
Practice motivational interviewing to explore her readiness to change and identify one small, realistic step she herself identifies

actions.name: 24-hour dietary recall
actions.result: Patient reports: coffee only in the morning (no breakfast food); snacks on chips, crackers, or pan dulce midday; dinner is often a frozen chicken alfredo tray or white rice with canned beans; drinks soda or sweetened iced tea through the day, little water; reports a 'big' late-night snack most nights but does not quantify it.

actions.name: Usual meal pattern and timing assessment
actions.result: Patient describes skipping breakfast most days, grazing on snacks through midday and afternoon, and eating her largest meal late at night, often after 9-10 pm.

actions.name: Fluid/beverage intake assessment
actions.result: Patient reports soda with most meals and sweetened iced tea between meals; says she drinks very little plain water, 'maybe a glass, if that.'

actions.name: Readiness-to-change / stage-of-change assessment
actions.result: Patient states she does not think her eating is a problem, says her labs 'aren't that bad,' and says she is here because her doctor sent her, not because she asked to come.

actions.name: Household and food access/barriers assessment
actions.result: Patient lives with five other people on different eating schedules; says cooking a full meal just for herself 'doesn't make sense'; relies on ready-made and frozen foods for convenience.

actions.name: Pain-related functional barriers to meal preparation
actions.result: Patient reports standing in the kitchen more than a few minutes brings on back pain and fibromyalgia soreness, which limits how much cooking she is willing to do.

actions.name: Review prior PCP nutrition intake note
actions.result: Note from a prior primary care visit documents patient self-report of 'eats three meals a day, no significant dietary concerns noted.'

actions.name: Review pharmacy refill history for acetaminophen
actions.result: Pharmacy refill log shows acetaminophen 325 mg tablets refilled monthly at a quantity consistent with near-daily use.

objectives.text: Elicit a focused diet history including meal pattern, typical foods, beverages, and portions to identify patterns relevant to prediabetes and weight management.
Identify practical and psychosocial barriers to healthy eating, including chronic pain limiting food preparation and the challenges of cooking for one in a crowded household.

Review relevant anthropometrics and laboratory data (BMI, HbA1c, fasting glucose, lipids, hemoglobin) and explain findings to the patient in plain, non-numeric language appropriate to her health literacy.

Reconcile discrepancies between the patient's current self-reported eating pattern and medication use versus prior documentation in the chart, exploring possible reasons without confronting the patient directly.
Formulate a nutrition diagnosis based on assessment findings, integrating diet history, barriers, and biochemical/anthropometric data.

Apply motivational interviewing techniques to explore a precontemplative patient's ambivalence about dietary change, gently uncover sensitive information about nighttime eating patterns, and collaboratively identify one small, realistic step she herself identifies.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive energy intake and irregular meal pattern (nighttime grazing/binge eating of energy-dense snack foods, skipped breakfast, heavy reliance on convenience/fast foods) related to chronic pain limiting food preparation, unresolved grief after 2023 pregnancy loss, and low health literacy; evidenced by BMI 30 kg/m2, A1c 6.4%, and self-reported eating pattern
differential: Nutrition diagnosis: Excessive energy intake related to nighttime binge eating and reliance on convenience/fast food, as evidenced by BMI 30 and A1c 6.4%

Nutrition diagnosis: Undesirable food choices related to limited cooking ability from chronic pain and low health literacy, as evidenced by diet history of frozen meals, fast food, and sugar-sweetened beverages

Nutrition diagnosis: Disordered eating pattern (nocturnal eating) related to unresolved emotional distress (2023 miscarriage), as evidenced by patient report of eating alone at night 'without noticing' and concealing wrappers

Not a nutrition diagnosis but a pertinent medical consideration: mild anemia (Hgb 11.2) that may contribute to fatigue reported by patient, not primarily nutrition-related today but worth noting for referral
keyFindings: BMI 30 kg/m2 (height 153.2 cm, weight 70.5 kg) consistent with obesity
A1c 6.4% (2026-02-18) and fasting glucose 83.4 mg/dL, consistent with prediabetes
Vitals 2026-02-18: BP 138/75, HR 80, RR 13 - unremarkable for this visit
Lipid panel 2024-02-07 within normal limits (TC 157.7, LDL 78.5, HDL 58.7, TG 103)
Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL (2024-02-14), mildly low, with pale conjunctiva/nail beds on exam
Diet history reveals skipped breakfast, grazing through day, large late-night meal, heavy reliance on frozen/fast food, soda/sweetened tea as primary fluids
Reluctant disclosure: nighttime consumption of large quantities of chips/cookies 'without noticing,' sometimes eaten alone to avoid partner seeing

Mismatch: pharmacy refill records show near-daily acetaminophen use and a prior nutrition note stating she 'eats three meals a day,' which conflicts with her current report of skipping breakfast most days

Hidden fact (only emerges with sustained rapport): nighttime eating began after her 2023 miscarriage as a way to fall back asleep, and she disposes of wrapper evidence outside rather than in household trash
plan: Complete a structured 24-hour recall/diet history and compare against prior documented intake note to gently reconcile the three-meals-a-day discrepancy
Review relevant labs (A1c, fasting glucose, lipids, hemoglobin) and vital signs in context of nutrition diagnosis, explaining results in plain, non-numeric language she can use
Formulate and document a PES-format nutrition diagnosis addressing excessive energy intake and nighttime eating pattern

Use motivational interviewing (open-ended questions, reflective listening, avoiding direct advice-giving) to explore her ambivalence about her eating and connect, at her pace, to how she already feels (pain, fatigue, sleep)

Identify one or two small, pain-compatible, culturally relevant behavior changes she identifies herself (e.g., a simple no-cook breakfast item, swapping one soda for water/agua fresca) rather than prescribing a full diet overhaul
Explore ways to redirect her partner's hovering toward practical support (e.g., grocery shopping) rather than monitoring, if she is receptive

Screen gently for nighttime eating pattern and associated distress; if disclosed, acknowledge supportively and consider referral to behavioral health/counseling for unresolved grief, without pressing for details beyond what she offers
Document anemia and fatigue findings for PCP follow-up; this is not the primary focus of today's nutrition visit
redFlags: Mildly low hemoglobin (11.2 g/dL) with pale conjunctiva/nail beds - warrants PCP follow-up though not acutely urgent
Patient minimizes/denies connection between diet and prediabetes despite clear precontemplation stage - risk of disengagement if lectured
Concealment behavior around nighttime eating (hiding wrappers outside the house) suggests shame/distress that may need behavioral health referral if she discloses more
History of pregnancy loss (2023) with eating behavior onset immediately after - possible unresolved grief, consider gentle referral if she is open to it
educationPoints: Explain A1c and glucose results in plain, non-numeric terms (e.g., 'your blood sugar is a little higher than it should be, but we caught it early and small changes can help') rather than citing percentages or reference ranges

Normalize that convenience and fast foods are not 'bad' but discuss simple ways to make them a little more balanced (adding a vegetable side, smaller portion from the tray) without requiring full home cooking
Discuss that sugary drinks (soda, sweetened tea) raise blood sugar more than water, using concrete comparisons rather than numbers (e.g., comparing to spoonfuls of sugar)
Validate that her back pain and energy level are real priorities, and frame nutrition changes as potentially helping her feel less tired or achy, rather than solely about weight or labs
Offer reassurance that nighttime eating is common and not something to feel ashamed of, if she discloses it, and that support is available without judgment
Discuss practical, low-standing-time food prep ideas (e.g., pre-portioned snacks, sitting while prepping) that respect her pain limitations

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports skipping breakfast most days, having only coffee, then grazing through the day and eating her largest meal late at night (a2, a1)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Prior PCP nutrition intake note documents patient self-report of 'eats three meals a day, no significant dietary concerns noted' (d2)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Dietary self-report can change over time or vary by context/rapport; reconcile discrepancies between current recall and prior documentation with curiosity rather than confrontation, since both may reflect the patient's honest perception at different moments.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports taking acetaminophen 325 mg as needed for pain, not on a fixed schedule, and feels it provides little relief but 'just takes it anyway' (h21, h22)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows acetaminophen 325 mg tablets refilled monthly at a quantity consistent with near-daily use (d3)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may underestimate or minimize how consistently they use a medication; refill records can reveal a pattern of near-daily use that differs from a patient's description of irregular, as-needed dosing, which is relevant context for her pain and sleep disruption affecting eating patterns.
